line: Good afternoon. Aurelio Mendoza. I'm with the Club Jerez, we meet here Thursday nights. You're new around here?
choice1: Yes, I'm {playerName}. I just moved in.
choice2: Nice to meet you, Don Aurelio.

line: Welcome. Sit, sit, the chairs are free. Are you looking for somebody, or just seeing the hall?
It's an old building. The roof leaks over the kitchen door, there's a raffle for that. The kitchen is good. Thursdays it smells like my wife's kitchen, because it's my wife cooking.
The Club. Families from Jerez, in Zacatecas. Forty-two families now. We eat, we argue, we plan the dance.
choice1: Where are you from, in Jerez?
choice3: Forty-two families. I'll let you go.

line: From the town itself, two streets from the market. I came here at nineteen, to work. Thirty-four years a pipefitter, union, in the boiler rooms under this city.
choice3: That's a lot of years. I should go.

line: Hospitals, schools, the courthouse. Every building on Fifth, I have been under it. Hot work. You come up at the end of the shift and it's winter.
choice1: And the Club, what does it do?
choice2: I'll think of that next time I'm on Fifth.

line: Money, mostly. Last year we paid for a new roof on the clinic in Jerez. Raffles, the dance, plates of food after Mass on Sundays.
choice3: Good for you. I'll let you go.

line: All by ourselves. No city, no grants, no forms. _straightens his belt_ My father was born in that clinic. Now it doesn't rain on the next ones.
choice2: That's something to be proud of.

line: Thirty-four years I worked in the city's buildings. I know how it goes. They give you a little, then they come with a clipboard. $ What's ours, we keep ours.
Maybe. I'll tell you what I see. The young ones who go to the programs across Grand, I don't see them here after. The Club needs people who come back.
Some do. When they have children, usually. They bring the baby to the dance so the grandmothers can hold it. Come to the dance, then we'll see if you come back.
Around the block. Past the bakery, past Ray's office with his name in the window, back to the side steps. Two laps. My wife counts.
Across Grand? For what. My bakery is here, my doctor speaks Spanish, my church is here. Thursday nights, the noise from the kitchen, that's us. The Club Jerez.
choice2: Sounds like a good side of the street.

line: Ah, {playerName}. You caught me going out. After lunch I walk, my wife's orders. Two laps, then the side steps. Come sit, I'm slow.
Look at those two on the steps. The same argument every Sunday after Mass, about the Chivas. Nobody ever wins.
choice3: I'll let you finish your lap.

line: Football? No, I argue, I don't play. In Jerez the men play dominoes, outside, and loud. At the Club we play on Thursdays after the meeting, and it's still loud.
choice2: Why not play in the park?

line: _looks across Grand, toward the park_ Over there the chess men would move to another bench. No. Thursdays at the hall, you watch first. Watching is how you learn the arguing.
Morning, {playerName}. You're early. The coffee's not ready, the urn is thinking.
Morning, {playerName}. You're early. The coffee's not ready, the urn is thinking.
Here? Pilar. Ask anybody. She has the keys and the calendar. I have Thursdays.

Thursdays are enough, if you use them right. She's good, Pilar. She talks to everybody, the library, the clinic, the city. Somebody has to. $ [guarded] But a hall that talks to everybody, who does it listen to? On Thursdays it listens to us. Come on a Thursday.
The families. And the families ask me. Forty-two of them, thirty-five years. The priest signs the papers, but first he calls me.

Pilar runs her Tuesdays, the class, the pantry. I don't get in her way. She asks before she brings the library people in, and mostly I say yes. $ Mostly. A hall is like a kitchen. Too many cooks from outside, and nobody knows where the pots go. You, come Thursday. Learn where the pots go.
choice1: I'll learn where the pots go.

line: The dance is in three weeks. The band from Fresno wants double this year.
I said, for double, play twice as long. They said no. The band from Fresno has no shame. You can repeat that, I said it first.
choice3: I'll let you work on it.

line: There's a boy, Chuy. His grandfather played in the Club band in the eighties. He has the trumpet and four friends. I'm thinking about it.
choice3: Let me know what you decide.

line: He's loud, that's most of it. And the grandmothers would cry to hear the grandfather's songs from the grandson. That's worth more than Fresno.
{playerName}. Sit a minute. I want to tell you something, and then you can tell me I'm an old man.
You talk to Pilar, you talk to Ray, I see you. Good. Listen to all of us.
Pilar wants to walk everybody across Grand, with the forms. Ray wants everybody to be Raymond. They're good people. They mean well.
I want there to be a here. A room where the Jerez families eat on Thursday. If everybody walks across Grand, who keeps the room?
choice2: Maybe there's room for all three.

line: Maybe. You're young, you can say that. Just come Thursday sometimes. Bring the questions, I like the questions.
Ah, {playerName}. Can I ask you something?
Saturday the Club's board has dinner at my house. My wife makes birria. Some of the young ones come, the ones who will run the Club after me. I want you sitting with them.
Because you keep coming back. That's the only qualification. The rest you learn from the treasurer.
Good afternoon. Sit. Somebody has the news on in the kitchen again.
Enough. I'm not surprised, and you shouldn't be. When Washington gets nervous, it's us they look at. It was like this in '96 too. I remember.
Raids at the meatpacking plant downstate. Two men from the Club, gone in one week. We collected money for their families in a coffee can.
choice3: That's hard. I'll let you be.

line: Now the Club has its own fund, for lawyers. Since 2006. Every family puts in a little every month. Nobody had to give us permission.
Alone, no. Forty-two families, yes. _folds his hands_ If somebody you know needs a lawyer, you tell me. Quietly.
Good afternoon. Everybody is happy today. The ladies are singing in the kitchen.
Let them enjoy. But you know why he won? Not because he's a nice man. Because people like us registered, knocked on doors, drove the grandmothers to vote. The Club alone drove forty cars that day.

Forty cars, from this parking lot. That's the lesson, {playerName}. Not the president, the cars. A community that holds together puts presidents like this in office. Scatter, and you get the other kind.
choice1: So nothing changes for the Club?

line: When they offer something now, fine, the hall can take it. I don't stop anybody. But the Club doesn't change its plans for Washington. Washington changes its plans for the Club.
Ah, {playerName}. You're here so much the ladies ask if you're somebody's nephew.
I tell them yes. Don't make me a liar.
When I came, I had nobody here. A man from Jerez, Don Tomás, gave me his couch and his cousin's phone number. That's how the Club started. Couches.
One family at a time. Somebody arrives, somebody calls me. We find a couch, a job, a church. Forty-two families. I know all the children's names.
Ah. They tell me you're at the library more and more.
choice1: I still come here, Don Aurelio.

line: No. It's a good library. My granddaughter goes, for the computers. They're polite over there. Polite is not the same as yours.
choice1: Does she come to the Club?

line: To the dance, yes. Otherwise she's busy. Her Spanish gets smaller every year. Her mother says don't push.
A little. Thursdays I bring her to the kitchen, and her grandmother talks to her only in Spanish. She complains. She answers. $ Just remember who fed you first, {playerName}. That's all.
Hm. You came back.
choice1: I spoke out of turn before. I'm sorry.

line: Good. A man who says sorry, I can talk to. Not today, maybe. But sit with me next time.
Ah, {playerName}. Good to see you. Did you eat?
Thursday there's food at the Club. Gorditas, my wife's. Come hungry. Or come full, she'll feed you anyway.
choice1: Remind me what the Club does?

line: Not now, I'm waiting for the treasurer. She's always late, and always right.
